hookLine: For thirty years, Alabama planned to execute him — for two murders he did not commit.

captions.text: For nearly thirty years, the state of
Alabama kept a date to kill Anthony Ray
Hinton —
for two murders he did not commit.
The entire case rested on a single bullet.
And that bullet, it turned out,
matched nothing at all.
This is the story of how one piece
of "science" and a broke defense sent an
innocent man to death row for nearly three
decades —
how the system almost killed him for it —
and how it never managed to take the
one thing that kept him alive.
In 1985, around Birmingham, Alabama,
two fast-food managers were murdered in
separate late-night robberies —
John Davidson in February, Thomas Wayne
Vason in July.
Both were killed for the cash in a
restaurant safe.
There were no eyewitnesses to either killing.
There were no fingerprints.
For months, the cases went nowhere —
and an unsolved murder of a working man
is exactly the kind of case a police
department badly needs to close.
Pressure to solve a killing is its own
kind of force; it bends everything toward
an answer, any answer that will hold.
Two men were dead.
A city wanted someone to pay for it.
And when the survivor of a third robbery
pointed to a face in a photo array,
the machinery of a capital case began to
move —
and it would not pause to ask whether
it had the right man.
Then, weeks later, a third restaurant was robbed.
This time the manager, a man named Sidney
Smotherman, survived being shot at —
and later picked a face out of a
photo lineup.
The face belonged to a
twenty-nine-year-old Black man named
Anthony Ray Hinton.
That identification is the only reason
Hinton entered this story at all.
There was nothing else tying him to the
first two murders —
no witness, no print, no confession.
Nothing except what the police believed a
gun could tell them.
But here is the fact the jury would
be asked to set aside.
At the moment of that third robbery,
Anthony Ray Hinton was fifteen miles away,
locked inside a supermarket warehouse,
working a night shift.
He was clocked in.
A supervisor could place him there.
His own time card could place him there.
He could not have been in two places
at once.
In almost any other case,
that is where a prosecution ends.
A man locked inside a warehouse,
on the clock, miles away,
is not your suspect.
But the state had already decided who it
was looking for —
and it believed it had found something
that could beat any alibi at all.
That something was the bullets.
Prosecutors claimed the bullets from the
crime scenes had been fired from an old
.38-caliber revolver that belonged to
Hinton's mother, recovered from her home.
There were no fingerprints.
No eyewitness who saw the murders.
No confession.
There were only those bullets,
and a gun that had sat,
for years, in an aging woman's house.
If the bullets matched that revolver,
the case was closed.
If they didn't, the state had nothing.
The entire question of whether a man would
live or die came down to a duel
between firearms experts.
And this is where being poor decides everything.
To fight the state's ballistics claim,
Hinton needed a real forensic expert of
his own.
But his court-appointed lawyer was working
under a belief that turned out to be
false: he thought Alabama law capped the
money for a defense expert at just one
thousand dollars.
There was no such cap.
The law would have paid for a qualified
expert, if he had only asked for it.
He didn't ask.
He took the thousand dollars,
and with it he hired the only person
willing to work for that price.
The man he found was a civil engineer
named Andrew Payne.
On the stand, under cross-examination,
Payne admitted that he had sight in only
one eye —
and that he could not properly operate the
comparison microscope, the very instrument
used to match a bullet to a gun.
The prosecutor took him apart in front of
the jury, piece by piece.
The one witness standing between Anthony
Ray Hinton and the electric chair could
not see, and could not work his own equipment.
Picture it: the man hired to defend a
capital case, squinting into an instrument
he could not operate, while the prosecutor
asked him again and again to explain what
he saw.
He could not.
And a jury watched the only science on
Hinton's side come apart in real time.
Understand what that thousand-dollar
mistake really was.
In a case built entirely on the science
of matching a bullet to a gun,
a man's life depended on having a
scientist who could actually do it.
The money was there for the asking.
His lawyer, wrongly believing it wasn't,
never asked.
That single unasked question is what sent
an innocent man toward death.
The jury took about an hour.
In September of 1986, they convicted him
of both murders, and he was sentenced to die.
Hinton always said what he believed put
him there.
He was Black.
He was poor.
He could not afford a defense that could
fight back.
And in Alabama, in 1986,
that was enough.
He would say later that he understood
exactly what he must have looked like to
that jury: a poor Black man from Alabama,
accused of killing two people,
with a broken-down witness for a defense
and a court-appointed lawyer who had not
fought for the money to defend him.
In a system like that,
he came to believe, the verdict was
written before the trial ever began.
And it is hard to argue with him.
The evidence was junk.
The defense was broke.
The jury was out for about an hour.
In that room, on that day,
the outcome had less to do with what
had happened than with who was standing accused.
He was sent to a cell the size
of a bathroom on Alabama's death row.
And he would stay there for the better
part of thirty years.
For the first three years,
he barely spoke —
swallowed by rage and grief at a system
that would not listen.
And then Anthony Ray Hinton made the
decision that is the heart of this story.
He decided that a cell could hold his
body, but it would not hold his mind.
He started a book club —
condemned men meeting among the law books
to argue about writers like James Baldwin.
In his imagination, he simply left.
He traveled the world.
He married movie stars.
He played center field for the New York Yankees.
He found humor in a place with no
reason for any.
You can lock up a man's body,
he understood.
You cannot lock up what he allows himself
to imagine.
There were seven of them in that book
club at the start —
condemned men passing paperbacks down the
row, arguing about the ending as if any
of them had all the time in the world.
They did not.
But for an hour, in a house of
the sentenced, a book could make the walls
disappear.
From the outside, that can sound like a
small thing —
a man telling himself stories to pass the time.
It was not small.
It was the difference between surviving
and being erased.
The state had taken his freedom,
his good name, nearly three decades of his
one life.
The single thing it could not reach was
the country he built inside his own head —
and he defended it like the last free
ground he had left.
But imagination is not innocence,
and the years kept coming.
He had founded that book club with a
handful of other condemned men —
and one by one, over the years,
he watched its members walked past his
cell to be executed, until he was the
last of them still breathing.
Over his decades on the row,
Hinton says he counted fifty-four men
taken to the electric chair,
close enough to know each one.
Any year, it could be his door.
He came to know the sound of it —
the particular quiet of the row on an
execution night, the footsteps, the smell
that followed.
One by one, the men of his book
club were taken, until Anthony Ray Hinton
was the only one of them left alive
to remember they had ever existed.
Then a lawyer named Bryan Stevenson,
and his Equal Justice Initiative,
took Hinton's case —
and would fight it for the next sixteen years.
Sixteen years spent trying to make a state
admit it had condemned the wrong man.
In 2002, Stevenson did the one thing
Hinton's first defense never could.
He put three of the most qualified
firearms experts in the country on the
stand —
one of them from the FBI —
and they testified, plainly, that the
crime bullets could not be matched to that
revolver.
They could not even be certain the bullets
had come from a single gun.
This was not a loophole or a clever defense.
It was the plain truth of the physical
evidence, told by the best in the field.
The one thread the entire death sentence
hung from had never actually held.
And still —
for more than a decade after that —
the state of Alabama refused to let him go.
In the end, it took the Supreme Court
of the United States.
In 2014, in Hinton v.
Alabama, the Court ruled —
and it was unanimous, nine to nothing.
Every justice agreed that Hinton's
original trial had been unconstitutional,
because his lawyer's failure to seek the
money for a real expert —
a failure built on that false belief about
a thousand-dollar cap —
had denied him a real defense.
The right to a lawyer,
the Court has always said,
means the right to a lawyer who does
the basic work.
In a case that lived and died on
expert testimony, asking for the money to
hire a competent expert was as basic as
it gets.
The verdict was thrown out.
The case was sent back.
And when the state finally had to prove
its ballistics match again, with modern
experts, it couldn't.
The evidence that had sent him to death
row simply could not be reproduced —
because it had never been true.
With no case left, prosecutors moved to
drop the charges.
It had taken sixteen years of Bryan
Stevenson's fight, and thirty years of
Anthony Ray Hinton's life, to undo a
one-hour verdict built on a bullet that
never matched.
On April 3rd, 2015, Anthony Ray Hinton
walked out of prison a free man,
after nearly thirty years —
the hundred-and-fifty-second person freed
from death row in America after being
wrongly condemned to die.
He stepped into the sunlight,
and he said the words that would become
the title of his book: the sun does shine.
He had walked into that cell at
twenty-nine years old.
He walked out at fifty-eight.
Nearly three decades —
the entire middle of a man's life —
spent a few steps from an execution
chamber, for a crime that was never his.
The two murders he spent thirty years
condemned for were never solved.
Think about what nearly killed him.
Not a lie anyone could see through at
a glance —
the opposite.
A neat, confident, official-sounding claim
that a bullet matched a gun.
It looked like science.
It looked certain.
And almost no one with the power to
stop it ever checked whether it was
actually true.
That is the quiet danger in this story.
The evidence that is most dangerous is not
the evidence that looks weak.
It is the evidence that looks certain —
because certainty is exactly what stops us
from looking closer.
Anthony Ray Hinton lost thirty years to a
bullet that matched nothing, and a defense
that could not see.
He walked out with his humor,
his imagination, and his life —
which, when a state spends three decades
trying to end it, is its own kind
of victory.
If a system could do this to an
innocent man, and very nearly get away
with it, hit like —
so that it's a little harder to look away.
